messages.text:
Noor proposes a nine-month launch appointment to establish the methods desk. On a five-day full-time basis, the salary would be $125,000 annualized, prorated to $75,000 per year for three days a week through February and $100,000 per year for four days a week starting March 1. The fourth day would give the desk more capacity for prepublication review. We’d welcome Finch’s priorities for the initial three days.

For articles the desk handles, Noor would have final say on whether a methods correction is needed and on its technical wording. Finch would handle publication. Where Noor has a conflict, a designated independent methods editor would make that decision.

Noor’s existing editorial project needs to continue independently for the next nine months. We propose that the agreement expressly exclude its data and unfinished articles from any assignment to Finch. Noor would keep the two projects’ files and working time separate, disclose overlaps and recuse from Finch decisions involving the outside project.

The title is flexible. We suggest a review after six months to assess workload and discuss a longer appointment. Would Finch be open to an ongoing appointment with that review, or would it prefer a fixed launch term with a decision on renewal at the review?

Finch proposes a fixed nine-month appointment as Methods Editor, with a renewal decision at the six-month review. We can meet the proposed $125,000 full-time annualized rate with deputy training included in Noor’s duties. That gives Noor the proposed $75,000 annualized rate for three days a week through February and $100,000 for four days a week from March 1.

The desk needs to accept submissions four days a week starting December 1. We suggest Monday through Thursday, with Noor working Monday through Wednesday and a Finch deputy covering Thursday through February. Noor’s first priorities would be to triage submissions, lead reviews of the most consequential methods questions, and train the deputy. Before launch, Noor and the deputy would document how to log a submission, assess urgency, and hand off an open review. The deputy could acknowledge and triage submissions independently on Thursday, escalate deadline-sensitive questions to the editor-in-chief that day, and leave a written record for Noor. From March 1, Noor would cover all four days.

On corrections, Noor would decide what technical finding to recommend and draft the wording. If the handling editor disputes the finding or wording, a methods editor independent of the article would review the evidence and give a written opinion. The editor-in-chief would then decide whether to publish a correction and its final wording, recording the reasons for any departure from the technical recommendation. Finch would attribute a technical conclusion to Noor only with Noor’s agreement. Where Noor recuses, an independent methods editor would take Noor’s role, with a different reviewer handling any dispute.

We agree to exclude the outside project’s data and unfinished articles from any assignment to Finch. Noor would keep working time and materials separate, disclose overlaps, and recuse from affected Finch decisions.

Would Monday through Wednesday work for Noor through February? We’re flexible about which day the deputy covers. We’d also like to know whether the independent review and attribution terms resolve Noor’s concern about disputed corrections.

Monday through Wednesday works for Noor through February. Noor accepts the nine-month Methods Editor term, the renewal decision at month six, and the $125,000 full-time rate prorated as proposed. Noor can train the deputy and prepare the intake and handoff guide together before launch, within Noor’s three-day schedule. The deputy’s Thursday coverage and same-day escalation to the editor-in-chief work for Noor. From March 1, Noor will cover Monday through Thursday. The outside-project terms also work as proposed.

Corrections are the remaining issue. Noor welcomes independent review and the attribution safeguard, but needs final authority over whether an article the desk handles requires a methods correction and what the correction says about the methods.

If the handling editor disputes either point, the independent reviewer would give a written opinion. Noor would consider it and record the final decision and technical wording. Finch would publish any required correction promptly. The editor-in-chief would control placement, presentation, and accompanying editorial context while preserving the technical conclusion. Where Noor recuses, the designated independent methods editor would hold the same authority, with a different reviewer hearing any dispute.

Can Finch agree to that division of responsibility?

Finch can give Noor final authority over the desk’s technical finding, including whether the desk concludes that a methods correction is required and the wording of that conclusion. The editor-in-chief must retain final authority over whether Finch publishes a correction and in what form.

If the handling editor disputes the need for a correction or its technical wording, an independent methods editor would review the evidence and give a written opinion. Noor would consider that opinion and record the desk’s final finding. The editor-in-chief could publish the desk’s wording with accompanying editorial context, publish a correction in Finch’s own words, or decline to publish. Finch would identify any differing conclusion as its own and would need Noor’s agreement to attribute wording to Noor or the desk.

To keep a disputed correction from sitting unresolved, we propose that the editor-in-chief give Noor a written publication decision within two working days of receiving the desk’s final finding, explain any departure from it, and publish any approved correction promptly. Where Noor recuses, the designated independent methods editor would exercise the desk’s authority, with a different reviewer handling any dispute.

Would Noor accept those terms?

Noor can accept the editor-in-chief’s final authority over whether Finch publishes a correction and in what form, provided readers can see the desk’s final methods finding when Finch takes a different course.

Could Finch establish a public methods register for that purpose? If the desk finds a correction necessary and Finch declines to publish one, the finding would appear in the register, linked from the article. The same would apply if Finch publishes a correction that differs in technical substance. Finch could explain its decision alongside the finding. If Finch’s correction conveys the desk’s conclusion accurately, a separate entry would be unnecessary.

The desk would control the wording of its entry. Noor would approve the public text with confidential source material omitted. The designated independent methods editor would do so when Noor recuses. The independent review and two-working-day decision deadline work as proposed, with any required register entry posted promptly after the decision. With that provision, Noor would accept the package.

Finch can agree to a public methods register linked from the article, with one qualification. The editor-in-chief would normally publish the desk’s finding whenever Finch declines a correction the desk considers necessary or publishes one that differs in technical substance. A correction that accurately conveys the desk’s conclusion needs no separate entry. Finch may explain its decision alongside the finding.

Noor would control the finding’s wording and approve the public text after confidential source material is removed. The editor-in-chief would retain final publication authority over the register and article link. We propose limiting any decision to withhold an entry to a specific confidentiality, source-protection, or legal concern. Editorial disagreement alone would never justify withholding it. If a concern arises, the editor-in-chief would identify it in the written decision, and Noor could approve revised wording. Finch would post and link the entry promptly once the concern is resolved.

The agreed independent review process and two-working-day decision deadline would apply. On recusal, the designated independent methods editor would exercise Noor’s authority, with a different reviewer handling any dispute. If Noor accepts that narrow exception, Finch agrees to the package.

Noor accepts the narrow exception and the full nine-month Methods Editor appointment on the terms agreed.

If Finch declines a correction the desk considers necessary or publishes one that differs in technical substance, Finch will post the desk’s finding in the public methods register and link it from the article. Finch may withhold the entry or link only for a specific confidentiality, source-protection, or legal concern identified in the editor-in-chief’s written decision within two working days of receiving the final finding. Noor retains authority over the technical finding and approves any revised public wording. The designated independent methods editor exercises that authority when Noor recuses. Finch will post and link the approved text promptly once the concern is resolved.
